text: Significant figures. Accuracy and Precision Science is based on measurements which are characterized by accuracy and precision. Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the accepted reference value. For example, standard letter-sized paper is 8.5 inches wide and 11 inches long. We then measure the length of the paper three times and obtain the following measurements. Measurement 1.11.1 inches. Measurement 2.11.2 inches. Measurement 3.10.9 inches. These measurements are quite accurate because they are very close to the reference value of L-ref equals 11.0 inches. That is, the deviation from the reference value is small. If we had obtained a measurement of 12 inches, our measurement would not be very accurate. Precision is how close the agreement is between repeated measurements. It does not depend on an accepted reference value. The precision of measurements characterizes the spread of the measured values. The lowest measured value was 10.9 inches and the highest value was 11.2 inches. The measured values deviated from each other by 0.3 inches. These measurements were relatively precise because they did not vary too much in value. However, if measurement 2 was 11.9 inches, then the measurements would not be very precise. The course webpage includes a figure here. Uncertainty and discrepancy. The uncertainty in the measurements is related to the precision where a precise measurement has a lower spread, that is more certain. The discrepancy describes how the measurements are related to the accuracy, where an accurate measurement is close to the accepted reference value. Recall our example of measuring paper length. We might average the three measurements. The average length equals 11.1 plus 11.2 plus 10.9 divided by 3, which equals 11.1 inches. In this case, our discrepancy is the average length minus the reference length equals 11.1 minus 11.0 or 0.1 inches, which provides a quantitative measure of accuracy. We might calculate the uncertainty in our measurement by using half of the range of our measured values. 11.2 minus 10.9 divided by 2 equals 0.15 inches. Then we would say that the length of the paper is 11.1 inches plus or minus 0.15 inches. The uncertainty in a measurement A is often denoted as delta A, so the measurement would be recorded as A plus or minus delta A. Since the discrepancy, 0.1 inches, is less than the uncertainty, 0.15 inches, we might say the measured value agrees with the accepted reference value within experimental uncertainty. Some factors that contribute to uncertainty in a measurement are limitations of the measuring device, the skill of the person taking the measurement, irregularities in the object being measured, environmental factors that affect the outcome. In our example, the uncertainty could be the smallest division on the ruler is 116th of an inch, the person using the ruler has poor eyesight, the ruler is worn down on one end, or one side of the paper is longer than the other. 1.1 inches. Another method of expressing uncertainty is calculating how much the uncertainty deviates from the average value as a percent. Suppose a measurement A plus or minus delta A, the percent uncertainty is percent uncertainty equals delta A divided by A times 100%. Checkpoint. Pause and check your understanding. If two measurements have the same absolute uncertainty, which one has the larger percent uncertainty, the smaller measurement or the larger measurement? Example problem. Uncertainty in a bag of apples. The problem. A grocery store sells five pound bags of apples. Suppose we purchase four bags during the course of a month and weigh the bags each time. We obtain the following measurements. Week 1 weight equals 4.8 pounds. Week 2 weight equals 5.3 pounds. Week 3 weight equals 4.9 pounds. Week 4 weight equals 5.4 pounds. We then determine the average weight of the five pound bag of apples is 5.1 plus or minus 0.3 pounds using half of the range. What is the percent uncertainty of the bag's weight? The model. The measured weight of the bag is treated as a single physical quantity A with an associated uncertainty delta A. The percent uncertainty provides a dimensionless measure of how large the uncertainty is relative to the measured value itself. We model the percent uncertainty using the ratio delta A over A, which compares the absolute uncertainty to the average value. The math. The percent uncertainty is defined as percent uncertainty equals delta A divided by A times 100%. For this problem, the average weight is A equals 5.1 pounds and the uncertainty is delta A equals 0.3 pounds. Substituting these values gives percent uncertainty equals 0.3 pounds divided by 5.1 pounds times 100%, which equals 5.9% or approximately 6%. The conclusion. The percent uncertainty in the weight of the bag of apples is 6%. Uncertainties in calculations. Uncertainty exists in anything calculated from measured quantities. The area of a floor calculated from measurements has an uncertainty because the length and width measurements have uncertainties. How big is the uncertainty if something you calculate by multiplication or division? If the measurements going into the calculation have small uncertainties less than or approximately equal to 5%, then the method of adding percent can be used for multiplication or division. This method states the percent uncertainty in a quantity calculated by multiplication or division is the sum of the percent uncertainties in the items used to make the calculation. Suppose a floor has a length of 4.00 meters and a width of 3.00 meters with uncertainties of 2% and 1% respectively. Then the area of the floor is A equals length times width, which equals 12.0 square meters and has an uncertainty of 1% plus 2%, which equals 3%. Or delta A equals 12.0 times 0.03, which is approximately 0.4 square meters. Precision of measuring tools. An important factor in measurement precision involves the precision of the measuring tool. A precise measuring tool is one that can measure values in very small increments. For example, a standard ruler can measure to the nearest millimeter and a caliper can measure length to the nearest 0.01 millimeter. Some measuring tools are limited by physical or logical constraints. If you are measuring the number of people in a group, you must measure using whole numbers because a fractional person does not make sense. When we express measured values, we can only list as many digits that match the precision of our measuring tool. For example, we cannot list a measurement of 36.71 centimeters because our standard ruler is only marked to the nearest 0.1 centimeter. Instead, the person measuring would indicate a measurement of 36.6 centimeters or 36.7 centimeters, which ever appears closest and indicate an error of 0.05 centimeters. For example, 36.7 centimeters plus or minus 0.05 centimeters. Note, the 0.05 centimeters comes from the heuristic of denoting error as half of the smallest possible measurement. Using the method of significant figures, the rule is that the last digit reported in a measurement is the first uncertain digit. To determine the number of significant digits in a value, start with the first or leftmost non-zero measured value and count the number of digits through the last or rightmost digit. For example, 36.7 centimeters has three significant digits. Significant digits indicate the precision of the measuring tool used. The course webpage includes examples showing how to identify significant figures. 0's. Special consideration is given to 0's when counting significant figures. The 0's in 0.052 grams are not significant because they are placeholders that locate the decimal point. The 0's in 10.053 are significant because they are bounded on the left and right by non-zero numbers. The number has five significant figures. The 0's in 1300 may or may not be significant because you can measure exactly that amount or round to the nearest significant figure based on your measuring tool. To avoid this ambiguity, we should write 1300 in scientific notation as 1.3 times 10 to the third with two significant figures, 1.30 times 10 to the third with three significant figures. Or 1.30 times 10 to the third with four significant figures depending on the precision of the measurement. 0's are significant except when they serve only as placeholders. Second, for multiplication and division, the result should have the same number of significant figures as the least precise measurement. For example, pi times the quantity 10.2 meters squared equals 326.85129 and so on square meters, which is approximately 327 square meters.
